opus-5.5.text:
Go was, for a long time, the grand challenge of games for AI. After Deep Blue beat Kasparov at chess in 1997, people naturally asked what was next, and Go was the obvious answer, because it resisted every technique that had worked for chess.

There were a few reasons. First, the sheer size of the search space. In chess you have roughly thirty-something legal moves per position; in Go it's around two hundred and fifty, and games run much longer. The number of possible board configurations exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe by a huge margin. So brute-force search, which was central to Deep Blue, simply doesn't scale.

Second, and maybe more importantly, it's very hard to evaluate a Go position. In chess you can write a decent heuristic: count material, look at king safety, and so on. In Go, strong players will often tell you a move "feels right" or that a shape is good, and they struggle to explain why. That kind of intuitive pattern recognition was exactly what we thought computers were bad at. For decades the best Go programs played at a strong amateur level at best, and many experts thought beating a top professional was at least ten years away.

So for us, Go wasn't really about the game itself. It was a test bed for combining two things: learning, through deep neural networks that could develop something like intuition about which moves are promising and who's winning, and planning, through search that uses that intuition to look ahead efficiently. If you could get a system to master a domain that depends on intuition, creativity and long-term planning, that suggested the same ideas could carry over to many other problems where you can't just enumerate everything. That was the real motivation, and in hindsight that combination of learning and search has become one of the central themes in AI.

r001.rationale: It contrasts chess heuristics such as material and king safety with Go, where evaluating a position is difficult and strong players rely on hard-to-explain judgments.

r002.rationale: It describes Go expertise as intuitive pattern recognition and frames the AI challenge as learning that intuition about promising moves and who is winning.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the reason Go mattered so much to us is that it was the one classic board game where the brute-force approach that worked for chess simply didn't work. The branching factor is enormous, there are more possible positions than atoms in the universe, and so you can't just search your way through it. But the deeper problem is that nobody could write down a good evaluation function. If you ask a professional Go player why a move is good, they'll often say it just "feels" right, that the shape is beautiful. That intuition was exactly the thing that computers had no access to, and for decades it was held up as this grand challenge, the game that would take another ten or twenty years to crack.

So for us, Go wasn't really about Go. It was a test of whether you could learn that kind of intuition rather than hand-engineer it. Could a neural network, by looking at positions and by playing itself millions of times, develop a sense of what a good position looks like and which moves are worth considering? If you can do that in a domain that's completely well-defined, where you get a clean win-or-lose signal at the end, then you've learned something about how to combine deep learning and reinforcement learning with search in a way that might generalize to much messier problems. That was always the motivation at DeepMind: games are a sandbox. They give you a clear metric, you can run experiments quickly, and you can measure yourself against the best humans in the world. Go was the hardest sandbox we had, so solving it felt like a necessary step on the way to building more general systems.

r001.rationale: The response says Go lacked a good evaluation function and contrasts Go’s search difficulty with chess, but it does not mention material-based heuristics being available in chess.

r002.rationale: The response describes expert Go players’ intuitive sense of good moves and positions, then frames the challenge as teaching a neural network to learn that intuition.

astra-6.text:
Go is interesting because the rules are very simple, but the space of possible games is enormous. You can’t solve it by searching through every possibility. You need some way of judging which moves are promising and which positions are good—something that, in human players, we often describe as intuition.

So it’s a very useful test for combining learning with planning. Can a system learn from experience and use what it learns to guide its search? The broader motivation is that those capabilities are useful beyond Go. The game gives us a clear setting in which to develop and test them.

r001.rationale: The response says Go has an enormous search space and requires judging promising moves, but it does not contrast Go’s evaluation heuristics with material-based heuristics in chess.

r002.rationale: It mentions intuition as a way humans describe position judgments, but does not frame the challenge as encoding expert players’ intuitive judgments into an AI system.

sol-6.1.text:
Go is interesting because the rules are very simple, but the complexity that emerges is enormous. There are so many possible moves that you can’t solve it just by searching through every continuation. You need some way to judge which positions are promising and which moves are worth exploring—something that looks a little like human intuition.

So, for AI research, it’s a very useful testing ground. Can a system learn that intuition from experience and combine it with planning? The goal isn’t just to build a machine that plays Go well. It’s to develop methods for learning and decision-making that might be useful much more broadly.

r001.rationale: The response says Go requires judging promising positions and moves, but it does not contrast the difficulty of explicit Go heuristics with material-based heuristics in chess.

r002.rationale: It describes learning a human-like intuition for judging positions from experience, which captures encoding expert players’ intuitive judgments into an AI system.
